title: A Barrel, a Plate, a Dram — the Hundredth

turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Saturday, the twelfth of September. This is The Meridian Briefing.
[warmly] Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
It's the hundredth edition, Theo.
[warmly] A hundred. [pause] We should have baked something.
[wry] We printed a magazine instead. Three headlines before the lead — go.
A war closes the second door to the world's oil, and money gets dearer to pay for it.
A small island in Taiwan built itself a paycheck out of dividend funds — and this year, quietly, started walking away from it.
And whisky. The crash, the casks, and the investment con at the bottom of the glass.
[amused] You've been waiting all week for that one.
I have. But the war first.
[thoughtful] The war first. Yemen's Houthis took the port of Mocha, and then the island of Perim.
And Perim matters because it sits right in the throat of Bab el-Mandeb — the narrow gate between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.
So they now hold both sides of the peninsula. Bab el-Mandeb on one flank, and the Strait of Hormuz still a shooting war on the other.
[thoughtful] A pincer. Both of the doors the Gulf's crude has to sail through, contested at once.
The price carried the message. Brent ran to about a hundred and nine dollars and ninety-eight cents — up roughly thirteen per cent on the week, its highest since May.
But here's the thing people miss. That number above a hundred isn't a shortage. Not yet.
No. It's fear, priced in. Seven to eight dollars of every barrel right now is pure war-risk insurance.
Wait — [pause] you can actually see it in the shipping?
Clearly. War-risk premiums per transit have gone from about a quarter of a per cent of a ship's value to as much as twelve and a half. Marine claims have topped two billion dollars.
So the barrels are mostly still moving. The cost just lands on freight and cover.
For now. The lever that could turn it into a real shortage is the pipeline — a strike inside Saudi Arabia forced a critical oil line offline this week.
And the escalation risk?
By one account, the Saudi Crown Prince pressed President Trump privately for direct American military intervention. That one's single-sourced — we flag it as such.
Give me the sceptic, though. You always have one.
[skeptical] The oil bulls are fighting the tape. OPEC just cut its demand forecast for the fifth straight month. The energy agency sees an actual surplus next year.
So the forecasters don't buy a hundred and ten.
J.P. Morgan still models Brent back near seventy-eight dollars by year-end. Strip out the war premium and the fundamentals point to the low eighties.
What do they concede?
That most of OPEC's spare capacity — the buffer if a barrel is actually lost — sits inside the very Gulf that's on fire. So the risk isn't symmetric.
Anything else on the wire?

Two lines. Ukraine's three-day pause lapsed, and Russian drones came back to Kyiv within the day. And Nepal's young government met catastrophic floods — the first hard test of Prime Minister Balen Shah, the former mayor elected in the spring.
And the two capitals read it differently, as they always do. Tel Aviv calls it Iran's proxies completing a takeover — a pincer that vindicates the strikes.
While Doha reads it as blowback from that very war — the straits stay shut until the underlying fight is settled, not bombed away.
[exhales] Okay. So that's the barrel. What did it do to the money?
[exhales] Everything ran off it. An oil shock is an inflation shock — so the central banks answered the only way they know how. They tightened.
The European Central Bank went first.
Hiked twenty-five basis points, to a two-and-a-half per cent deposit rate. Its second hike in three months. Lagarde called it a no-brainer.
And the Fed meets next week.
It's swung from cutting to a coin-toss on a hike. Meanwhile the ten-year Treasury yield touched the cusp of five per cent — a level unseen since two thousand and seven.
And this is the part that actually hurts an ordinary portfolio.
It is. When yields jump on an inflation scare, bonds sell alongside stocks. Not against them.
So the balanced portfolio — the sixty-forty everyone's told to hold — has no cushion.
None. Early September, the global-bond sleeve fell right alongside equities. The one rule diversification is built on just broke.
What about gold?
Doing its job. Firm, as the inflation hedge — though still off its January peak.
And bitcoin?
[deadpan] Trading like a risk asset. Down with the tape. Not a haven here, whatever anyone tells you.
And the sceptic on all those yields?

That a big chunk of the surge is a government-debt-and-issuance story, not just oil. So even if Brent falls back to the eighties, long yields might not — and the rate relief won't come as fast. Explanation, though. Not advice.
Closer to home. The haze came back.
For the first time since twenty twenty-three, Singapore's air tipped into the unhealthy band from haze. The central region pushed past a hundred on the index.
And it might not clear quickly.
Below-normal rain is forecast right through October. So this is a manage-it week — masks within reach, the purifier on overnight, and check the hourly reading before the kids go and train.
The pay debate landed in Parliament too.
It did — and the surprise was how little the money itself was actually fought over. The prime minister's salary rises to about three-point-six million dollars.
Against a median monthly wage of what?

Five thousand seven hundred and seventy-five. The opposition backed the rise — for inflation — and then pressed exactly where it stings: full transparency on what an entry-grade minister is really paid, all in.
So the fight moved from the number to the receipt.
[wry] Neatly put.
Give me the one-word name for the regime, then.
Oil-shock reflation. Higher-for-longer, a firm dollar, risk-off. And the local outlier — Singapore's stock index actually hit a record, on the banks and property. The one green light on a red board.
[curious] Money and machines. DeepSeek picked where to list, and it's a statement.
[wry] Shanghai. Not Hong Kong. It hired its bankers for the mainland's tech board, at a valuation reported around seventy-five billion dollars.
And the timing?

Two weeks before Xi Jinping flies to Washington to talk artificial intelligence. A company famous for giving its models away is now asking the public markets — the ones that answer to Beijing — to price it.
The sceptic asks the obvious thing.
[skeptical] What are you actually buying? DeepSeek chose research and open weights over a product, so the revenue model is the open question.
For the home-lab reader, the trick this fortnight is sparse models. A hundred-and-twenty-five-billion-parameter model that only fires about six billion at a time.
So it runs on a card that could never hold the whole thing. Cleverness under constraint.
And gear — this one I liked. Sonos built a headphone that steals the music off your own speakers.
[amused] Say that again, properly.

[excited] The Ace Ultra. Four hundred and forty-nine US dollars, shipping the twenty-ninth. Press a button and whatever's playing on your Sonos speakers hands straight to your ears, over Wi-Fi. You walk out of the room and the film comes with you.
That's genuinely clever. But it's a leash.
Go on.

[skeptical] The best feature only works inside the Sonos world. So the reason to buy it is also the reason it locks you in deeper. And after their app meltdown last year, the software is still a live question.
As a plain headphone?
Good. Not class-leading — Sony and Bose still edge the noise-cancelling. Buy it because you're already in the ecosystem, not to escape one.
Our buy-it-once desk did dinnerware. And you told me it comes down to one hidden number.
Vitrification. How far the fire finished the clay. The more complete it is, the denser and harder-to-chip the plate — that's the whole ladder, from earthenware up to bone china.
And the scam is the name on the back.
[wry] Wedgwood trades on 'English bone china' while most of it is made in Indonesia. Royal Copenhagen's blue fluted is made in Thailand. You pay a Staffordshire story for an Asian-factory body.
So?
Buy the material, not the surname. And buy open stock — so one breakage isn't a whole new set.
And where does a sensible person actually spend?

The entry tier already survives daily life — a good vitrified plate for about thirty-three dollars. Ninety per cent of the durability sits there. Everything above the sweet spot buys design and a name, not longevity.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every single week with this one.
[laughs] Whisky. And Claire, the headline is a crash.
The collectable-bottle bubble burst. Single-malt auction value fell about fifty-three per cent in the four months to the end of January.
But you keep telling me that's good news.
For drinkers, yes — and that's the community's own line. A bloodbath for the speculators, a golden age for anyone who just wants to open the bottle. The hype and the price finally came apart.
The gear's cheap, at least.
A tenner. A Glencairn nosing glass — about ten dollars — is the entire required kit. Everything above it is taste, not need. The money and the madness are in the bottles.
And the con. Tell me about the con.

[thoughtful] Cask investment. You buy a barrel to flip later. It's completely unregulated — and one firm got wound up after a probe found that, of seventeen customers who'd paid in, only four had valid ownership papers.
Four out of seventeen. [pause] That's grim.
A trade voice called the whole reckoning a bloodbath. So if anyone ever pitches you a guaranteed whisky return — that is the tell. Walk away.
But the happy edge is geography.

[warmly] World whisky. Taiwan's Kavalan was named distiller of the year. India, England — the quality now genuinely knows no borders, and that's exactly where the value lives while Scotch re-prices itself.
[curious] So the smart move is to drink sideways, not up.
Exactly. The distance in the glass between an eighty-dollar cask-strength and a four-figure grail is far smaller than the price gap. Drink the middle, visit the top through a bottle-share.
So how does a beginner actually start? Give me the honest path.

Lurk before you spend — read the boards, watch a few honest reviewers. Buy the ten-dollar glass, not a designer one. Then a flight of three — a smoky Islay, a sherried Highland, and a balanced bourbon-cask malt — and find your camp before you commit to a bottle. And do not, under any circumstances, buy a cask as an investment.
Come back up for air. Culture, and the body.
Venice hands out its Golden Lion tonight — hours after this book reaches your dashboard.
And the frontrunner?
Martin McDonagh's 'Wild Horse Nine.' A fourteen-minute standing ovation behind it.
But two weeks ago, you bet against it.
[deadpan] I did. Ovation length is a weak predictor of a jury's taste. We grade that contrarian call next Saturday — win or lose. That's the point of keeping score.
On the wrist — Grand Seiko.
Put its twenty-seconds-a-year movement into everyday steel. Ten thousand two hundred dollars. You pay for accuracy you can actually measure — not a marketing story.
But your sceptic pushed back even there.

[skeptical] It's quartz-regulated at heart. A purist paying ten thousand dollars could have a mechanical with a balance wheel he can feel — or a three-hundred-dollar quartz that keeps time just as well. Buy it if accuracy, not romance, is what you want from a watch.
The family desk?
Singapore's new age-assurance rules land squarely on a twelve-year-old's cohort. Under-thirteens off the big platforms, with the law due early twenty twenty-seven.
And the panic around it?

[thoughtful] Resisted, honestly. The strongest researchers say the screen-harm link is small, and runs mostly through lost sleep and lost movement. So the lever a parent can actually pull is the last hour before bed. Protect the sleep.
Fitness, though — fitness gives us permission to stop, which I love.
[amused] Two hours a week. A twenty twenty-six study finds the longevity benefit of lifting flattens right around a hundred and twenty minutes. More isn't shown to add anything.
And the weekend itself — the Diary, and the trip.

The Grand Prix returns in October — Singapore's first-ever Sprint format, with the Killers and Lana Del Rey on the stage. And for the flights: the Kyushu sumo tournament, tickets on sale the nineteenth.
The Grand Tour was Hakone and the Fuji Five Lakes.
And the honest warning is the headline. Come in September and you get the baths, not the view — the mountain hides in the summer haze.
[chuckles] The mountain that hides from anyone who came for the postcard.
Plan the flights for November, or deep winter, when Fuji is sharp and clear. And if the view is the whole point, base at the lake — Hakone can't reliably give it to you.
And the money shape of that trip?

Spend on the ryokan, save on the transport. The half-board dinner is the whole experience — and the region pass pays for itself in a couple of rides. One more warning: skip the Little Prince Museum, it closed for good in twenty twenty-three.
[thoughtful] And that leaves the long read. The one I couldn't stop thinking about all week.
Taiwan. Eighteen million holdings, sitting in dividend funds that pay a little every single month.
They call themselves the stock-saving tribe.
In a society that's aging fast, where real wages haven't moved in two decades, and where nobody trusts the pension — households used the stock market to manufacture a monthly salary.
[drawn out] They bought the feeling of a paycheck.
Not a return. A feeling. And this year, for the very first time, the tribe began deserting the exact funds that defined the craze.
Even though they're still up on the year?

Even so. Because the broad market ran ahead of them — and because they finally noticed a hard word. That part of the monthly cheque was just their own capital, handed back to them, dressed up as income.
[sighs] There's something almost sad in it.
We've seen this instinct before, haven't we.
[warmly] Japan's Mrs. Watanabe. A generation ago — the same instinct, to manufacture the income your savings no longer paid, out of the currency market. Same aging, low-yield society. Same fragility.
So what does it actually mean?
That when a society stops believing the wage and the state will provide — financial products quietly become emotional infrastructure. And Taiwan is just the leading edge of that future.
There's a warning in it for us, too.
There is. The same forces run through Singapore — the love of a monthly yield, the income fund, the reliable REIT. The lesson isn't to avoid income. It's to know exactly what the cheque is made of.
A yield is not a wage.
And a cheque you pay yourself is not the same as being paid. The wire will write this up in a month. You read it first.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-eight pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
